title: A Major Superconductor 'Speed Limit' Was Just Broken
excerpt: Superconductors give us sci-fi-worthy technologies like levitating trains, Big-Bang-replicating particle colliders, and medical machines that reveal our innermost secrets – thankfully only the physiological ones and not, perhaps, a secret love of polka dance.
content:
Superconductors give us sci-fi-worthy technologies like levitating trains, Big-Bang-replicating particle colliders, and medical machines that reveal our innermost secrets – thankfully only the physiological ones and not, perhaps, a secret love of polka dance.

But superconducting states are fragile. Materials must be cooled to very low temperatures, approaching the dark frigidity of outer space, to conduct electricity without resistance and subsequent energy loss.

The strength of the electrical current and of external magnetic fields can also snap these materials out of their superconducting states, as a curious cat's whisker or mistimed sneeze can knock down a precarious series of dominos.

Yet there's an even higher limit that's difficult to measure via conventional means, like direct current (DC) transport, because it's preempted by quantum disruptions that occur in just billionths of a second.

This is the depairing limit, where the entangled pairs of electrons, called Cooper pairs, that yield superconductivity are ripped apart. 

But in a breakthrough study published in Nature Physics, researchers smashed a superconductor 'speed limit' to probe this depairing, zipping past the disruptive quantum processes like a Formula 1 racer zooming past a Model T with a wonky wheel.

Unlike type I superconductors, which are generally pure metals and not so technologically useful due to their especially fragile magnetic limits, type II superconductors comprise a physical compromise:

They have higher magnetic thresholds because they allow internal magnetic fields to propagate as tiny tornadoes of electricity, called quantum vortices, keeping them in a superconducting state in more extreme conditions.

However, when an electric current running through a type II material becomes too strong, it whips up the tiny tornadoes, causing them to move, generating resistance and heat that stops superconductivity. 

"Our strategy was to outrun the vortex dynamics," conceptualizes lead author Eryin Wang, a physicist at the Max Planck Institute for the Structure and Dynamics of Matter (MPSD) in Hamburg, Germany. 

The researchers compared two superconducting materials, including niobium nitride (NbN) and a member of the yttrium barium copper oxide (YBCO) family of superconductors that exhibit 'high-temperature superconductivity'. 

They chose these materials because the former has an s-wave gap symmetry and the latter has a d-wave gap symmetry. This property dictate how easy it is to rip apart their paired electrons and therefore snap them out of their superconductive states.

But how does one outrun quantum processes, which exist at the limits of physics? By developing an optical-electric circuit that outpaces the velocity of the vortices – which act at tens of kilometers per second – by multiple orders of magnitude.

This setup shot ultra-quick laser pulses of green light lasting just 300 femtoseconds, or quadrillionths of a second, at a switch that turned the optical laser pulse into an electric current pulse that lasted picoseconds, or trillionths of a second (a relative slowpoke in comparison).

This is much quicker than the vortex dynamics could cause resistance and heat and the loss of superconductivity. 

In other words, a real quantum tortoise and hare situation, but one in which the hare is off the starting blocks while the tortoise is still having breakfast (perhaps the fox judging the contest was surreptitiously slipped a few eggs to overlook this 'inconsistency').

"Our results suggest that picosecond transport can provide access to microscopic properties of superconductors, including their gap symmetry, that are not directly available from conventional DC transport," explains Andrea Cavalleri, leader of the Condensed Matter Dynamics group at MPSD.   

Specifically, the NbN retained its superconductive state until the applied electric current reached a well-defined threshold, the researchers note, which is well above the conventional DC output because it's of such a short duration. At this point, its Cooper pairs fell apart and its superconductivity abruptly stopped. 

The YBCO material, on the other hand, displayed a gradual weakening of its superconductive state. This difference arises due to their different gap symmetries. 

The s-wave of the NbN has an energy gap (the energy needed to disentangle Cooper pairs) that's the same in all directions of momentum space.

But in YBCO, the energy gap varies significantly and even disappears in certain directions of momentum space. 

In other words, the former goes all-in on one poker hand, while the other may prefer to lose its money more slowly. 

The researchers thus got to the very fundamental root of superconduction, the stability of a material's Cooper pairs, the core quantum concept whence other effects emerge. 

The "novel approach" presented herein offers a framework for testing the key properties of superconducting materials, and thus 'zapping' a greater variety of superconductors can reveal properties like gap symmetries and how the materials react on their fundamental timescales. 

As summarized by Jianqiao Meng, a professor of physics at Central South University, who was not involved in this work, sometimes the race really does go to the swift:

"This work highlights the potential of ultrafast current pulses as a powerful new tool for accessing intrinsic superconducting properties." 

The research has been published in Nature Physics.
